Annual hospitalization rates for laboratory-confirmed influenza decrease with increasing age. For children under 6 months, the rates range from 240 to 720 per 100,000, while for children aged 2 to 5 years, the rates are approximately 20 per 100,000. 3. Children under 5 years of age with high-risk medical conditions have hospitalization rates of approximately 250 to 500 per 100,000. 4. Influenza-associated deaths are uncommon among children. During the 1990s, an estimated annual average of 92 influenza-associated deaths occurred among children under 5 years of age, compared to 32,651 deaths among adults aged 65 years or older. 5. During the 2003-2004 influenza season, 153 laboratory-confirmed influenza-related pediatric deaths were reported. Of these, 63% occurred in children under 5 years of age, and 40% occurred in children under 2 years of age. 6. Among 149 children who died and for whom underlying health information was available, 67% did not have a medical condition that would have indicated vaccination at the time. 7. These data suggest that while children with risk factors for influenza complications are at higher risk of death, the majority of pediatric deaths occur among children with no known high-risk conditions. 8. Since 2004, deaths associated with laboratory-confirmed influenza virus infection in children (defined as persons under 18 years of age) have been a nationally reportable condition. 9. During the 2004-2005 influenza season, the annual number of seasonal influenza-associated deaths among children under 18 years of age reported to the CDC ranged from 47 in 2004-2005 to 88 in 2007-2008. 10. During the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, over 300 deaths attributable to laboratory-confirmed H1N1 influenza among children were reported to the CDC in the United States. The majority of these children had one or more underlying medical conditions. 11. Deaths among children attributed to co-infection with influenza and Staphylococcus aureus, particularly methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), have increased. Co-infection is associated with greater illness severity compared to influenza alone. 12. The increase in co-infections may reflect a rising prevalence of MRSA colonization in the general population, with some strains carrying specific virulence factors. 13. Among healthy younger adults, seasonal influenza typically causes mild illness and rarely results in hospitalization, unlike in children under 5 years, adults aged 65 years or older, pregnant women, or individuals with chronic medical conditions. 14. However, influenza illness among healthy adults aged 19-49 years is a significant cause of outpatient medical visits and work absenteeism. 15. The impact of influenza varies considerably by season, making it challenging to estimate attack rates in healthy younger adults. Most studies report annual attack rates ranging from 2% to 10%, with an estimated 0.6 to 2.5 workdays lost per illness. 16. In one economic analysis, the average annual burden of seasonal influenza among adults aged 18-49 years without high-risk medical conditions included approximately 5 million illnesses, 2.4 million outpatient visits, 32,000 hospitalizations, and 680 deaths. 17. Hospitalization rates during typical influenza seasons are significantly higher for adults aged 65 years or older compared to younger age groups. 18. Retrospective analysis of data from managed-care organizations during 1996-2000 estimated that adults aged 65 years or older with underlying conditions had a hospitalization rate of approximately 560 per 100,000 during influenza seasons, compared to 190 per 100,000 for healthy individuals in the same age group. 19. Adults aged 50-64 years with underlying medical conditions also had substantially increased hospitalization rates during influenza seasons compared to healthy adults in the same age group. 20. Influenza is a major contributor to the annual increase in deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza observed during the winter months. 21. Between 1976 and 2001, an estimated annual average of 32,651 influenza-related deaths occurred among adults aged 65 years or older, with the highest risk in the oldest age groups. 22. Adults aged 85 years or older were 16 times more likely to die from influenza-related illness compared to those aged 65-69 years. 23. During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, adults under 65 years of age were at higher risk for influenza-related complications, particularly those aged 50-64 years with underlying medical conditions, compared to typical influenza seasons. 24. The distribution of hospitalizations by age group during the 2009-2010 influenza season differed from usual seasonal patterns, with more hospitalizations among younger age groups and fewer among adults aged 65 years or older. 25. Pneumonia with evidence of invasive bacterial co-infection was reported in approximately one-third of fatal cases in autopsy studies. 26. In one study of critically ill adults requiring mechanical ventilation, Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia at admission was an independent risk factor for death. 27. Obesity, particularly morbid obesity (BMI ≥ 40), appeared to be a risk factor for hospitalization and death in some studies during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. 28. Additional studies are needed to determine whether obesity is a specific risk factor for 2009 H1N1-like influenza viruses or a previously unrecognized risk factor for complications caused by other influenza viruses. 29. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic highlighted racial and ethnic disparities in the risk for influenza-related complications among adults, including higher hospitalization rates for Black individuals and a disproportionate number of deaths among American Indians/Alaska Natives and indigenous populations in other countries. 30. These disparities may be partially attributable to a higher prevalence of underlying medical conditions or disparities in medical care among these racial/ethnic groups. 31. Influenza symptoms are prolonged, and illness severity is increased among individuals with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. 32. A retrospective study of women aged 15-64 years enrolled in Tennessee's Medicaid program found that the attributable risk for cardiopulmonary hospitalizations among women with HIV infection was higher during influenza seasons than before or after influenza circulation. 33. The risk for hospitalization was higher for HIV-infected women than for women with other underlying medical conditions.
